name: Grace Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing civil engineering, which is bridges, drainage and a lot of maths I'm still wrestling with. I live at home with my parents and my grandmother, and I'm up at four three mornings a week to work at a bakery before lectures. Sundays are church and then Sunday lunch with the whole family. I'm the first one in my family at university, so everyone watches how I'm getting on, and that's a lot of pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because people were getting carried away. Real work is done by people who turn up and know what they're doing. I'd tell friends that a degree and good character still count for more than any gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, but my worries don't go away. I'm the first in my family at university, so I can't afford to fail, and my grades are only average. The bakery pay is small and the loan is big, and I'm very conscious that my parents are proud of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the same routine. Early shifts, lectures, labs, church. I'd ask my lecturers for extra help with the maths, and I'd try to find a summer job on a building site or with the council, to get a feel for the real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, but a bit weighed down. I carry my family's hopes around with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you carry your family's hopes. What does that feel like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small things. My mum tells her friends I'm training to build bridges. I can't tell them I'm struggling with a module, so I just study longer. My grandmother keeps asking about exam dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if you did fail a module?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retake it in the summer and not tell anyone until it was fixed. It would cost fees I don't have, and I'd have to pick up another bakery shift.

say: Real work is done by people who **turn up** and know what they're doing.
A **degree** and good character still count for more than any gadget.
think: I can't afford to **fail** as the first in my family at university.
The bakery pay is small and the **loan** is big.
do: **Keep** the routine of early shifts, lectures, labs and church.
Ask lecturers for extra **maths help** and look for a summer site job.
feel: **Settled** but weighed down by my family's hopes.
S0.quote: My mum tells her friends I'm training to build bridges. I can't tell them I'm struggling with a module, so I just study longer.
fieldNote: The pressure is **family pride**, not AI, and it shapes every answer.
She would **hide** a failed module until it is fixed.
Her faith and routine give her **structure** but also add to the weight.

steps.text: Keep the three early bakery shifts every week
Ask lecturers for extra help with the maths module
Look for a summer job on a building site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a lot of talk, and it'll change the office side of things first. I'd tell people that hard work still matters and that you should look after your own household before chasing trends. I don't think everyone needs to use a robot to write their emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm worried it takes away entry jobs, like the junior engineer who checks the drawings and does the calculations. That's the first rung on the ladder. But engineering on the ground, like surveying and site supervision, seems safer to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean towards the site side, applying for placements with building firms and the council. I'd keep studying hard on the basics, and I'd try learning one of the software tools properly if the course makes me, but I wouldn't go looking. I'd also keep the bakery job for the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious. I don't like being rushed, and this is a rushed sort of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't go looking for the software. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like handing my thinking to a machine. If I have to, I'll learn it on the job, with someone showing me. I'd rather understand the calculation than get an answer from a box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should help young people at this point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Employers, first. Take on apprentices and trainees, the way they used to. And families and churches, because a person needs support around them as well as a course.

say: Hard work still matters, and you should look after your own **household** first.
Not everyone needs a robot to write their **emails**.
think: The **junior engineer** rung of the ladder, checking drawings, is at risk.
Site work like **surveying** and supervision seems safer.
do: Apply for **placements** with building firms and the council.
Keep studying the **basics** and learn software only if the course requires it.
feel: A bit **anxious**, because I don't like being rushed.
S1.quote: I'd rather understand the calculation than get an answer from a box.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** to AI tools is moral as well as practical.
She trusts **employers, families and churches** more than the state.
Site work is her **safe ground**, the thing she steers towards.

steps.text: Apply for placements with building firms and the council
Practise hand calculations before using any software
Keep the bakery job for steady money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much too fast, and we should pray that leaders act wisely. I'd say people should look after their families and not be afraid to keep their feet on the ground. I'd also say it's not right for a few companies to gain from something that harms so many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. My degree could be pointless by the time I'm done, and the loan wouldn't go away. Hands-on work lasts until about 2031, and it takes a while for robots to be as good at building as people. But even that is not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents and my pastor, because I'd need advice from people I trust. I'd think about leaving for a building apprenticeship, since a trade has pay, and I know people who'd take me on. I'd stay at home, keep the bakery shifts and save every spare coin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid, honestly, but not frozen. I'd keep working and keep praying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people you trust. Who exactly would you go to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle runs a small building firm, and he's said before that he'd take me on if I wanted. He'd tell me straight whether the work is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your family react if you left the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would cry a bit, then say the right thing. My dad would say a trade is honest work. My grandmother would say whatever I do, do it well. They'd be fine, in the end.

say: It's **too much too fast**, and a few companies shouldn't gain while many suffer.
People should look after their **families** and keep their feet on the ground.
think: My degree could be **pointless** by the time I'm done, and the loan stays.
Hands-on work lasts until about **2031**, but even that isn't forever.
do: Talk to my **parents and pastor** and ask my uncle about a building apprenticeship.
**Keep** the bakery shifts, stay at home and save every spare coin.
feel: **Afraid** but not frozen, so I'd keep working and keep praying.
S2.quote: My uncle runs a small building firm, and he's said before that he'd take me on if I wanted.
fieldNote: Trust runs through **people she knows**, her uncle and pastor, not institutions.
Leaving the degree is a **real option**, backed by an offer from family.
Her fear is **steadied** by faith and family.

steps.text: Ask my uncle about a building apprenticeship
Talk to my parents and pastor about leaving the degree
Keep the bakery shifts and save every spare coin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and wise people will use it. I'd tell people to get proper skills they can do with their hands and heads. I'd say that employers should hire young people and train them, not leave them on the shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel steadier. By 2029 I'd have finished, and I could try to get into a job on site before the robots catch up around 2034. I'd also have a few years to build a name for being reliable, which matters more than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and spend each summer working on sites with my uncle. I'd aim for a site engineer role at a firm that builds roads or houses. I'd learn the software when someone shows me, and save a little for a small deposit on a flat when I'm ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, a bit cautious. I'd rather prepare quietly than shout about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being reliable matters. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a firm will keep someone who turns up on time and tells the truth. In my bakery, the owner's trusted me with the keys already. That counts for a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If firms stopped hiring juniors on site too, I'd go for a trade licence. A plumber or a bricklayer can still earn a living, and I'd rather have a skill than a title.

say: Five years is a fair warning, and wise people will **use it**.
Employers should **hire and train** young people, not leave them on the shelf.
think: By 2029 I could be on **site** before robots catch up around 2034.
Being **reliable** will matter more than people think.
do: Finish the degree and work **summers** on sites with my uncle.
Aim for a **site engineer** role and save for a small deposit.
feel: **Hopeful** but cautious, because I'd rather prepare quietly than shout.
S3.quote: A firm will keep someone who turns up on time and tells the truth. In my bakery, the owner's trusted me with the keys already.
fieldNote: She turns **character** into a career asset, in line with her traditional values.
She has a **trade licence** fallback if site jobs shrink.
Quiet **preparation** is her style, not protest.

steps.text: Work summers on sites with my uncle's building firm
Save for a flat deposit from bakery and site wages
Apply for site engineer trainee posts in third year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and I'd hope people use it to build things that last. I'd tell friends to focus on character and work they can be proud of. I'd say families and communities have to look after each other through the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine. By 2036 I'd be 28, perhaps married, with a job and a small place of my own. Robots come about 2039, and building is one of the hardest things for them. I'd be established by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work on site, and get qualified as a chartered engineer. I'd save for a deposit and help my parents with their bills as they get older. I'd learn AI tools slowly, if my job needed them, and I'd keep my faith and community at the centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, mostly. A long road is something I'm used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be different from today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less money stress. I'd like not to count coins on the bus. And I'd like my parents to have a bit of ease, since they've worked so hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What happens to people who don't have a trade or a church. Without a community, change like this hurts more. I'd like us to look out for them.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, and I hope people use it to build things that last.
Families and communities have to **look after** each other.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28, with a **job** and a small place of my own.
Building is one of the hardest things for **robots**.
do: Finish the degree and become a **chartered engineer** on site.
**Help** my parents with bills as they get older.
feel: **Peaceful** mostly, because a long road is something I'm used to.
S4.quote: Without a community, change like this hurts more. I'd like us to look out for them.
fieldNote: Her **worry** shifts from herself to people without a trade or a church.
She sees **community** as the main protection against change.

steps.text: Become a chartered engineer after three years on site
Help Mum and Dad with their bills as they age
Save toward a deposit for a small flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to find a safe path and I'd still owe my loan. What would help is employers taking on young people again, proper apprenticeships, and people in my church and family looking out for each other. And no one pretending it's easy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'm proudest of. When I got into university, my grandmother cried and then told me to work hard and stay humble. I don't want to let her down, whatever happens with the machines.

headlineQuote: When I got into university, my grandmother cried and then told me to work hard and stay humble.
portrait: Grace is 18, studies **civil engineering**, lives with her parents and grandmother and starts bakery shifts at four in the morning.
She is traditional, trusts **family, church and employers**, and avoids AI tools unless someone shows her.
She is the first in her family at university, so the **pressure** to succeed shapes her mood.
Her mood stays uneasy or anxious, and her fallback is a **building trade** through her uncle.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because there is no time to find a safe path.
whatWouldHelp: Employers taking on **apprentices** and trainees again.
Family and **church** looking out for each other.
